title: Improve How You Improve: Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Navigation
why: A-type recursive self-improvement harness for zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation that revises both the navigation program and the revision mechanism itself, requesting diagnostic views when observations cannot distinguish causes, and conditionally inheriting accepted program updates and spatial memory across goals.
mechanism: RPSI-Nav diagnoses search behavior, requests diagnostic views when existing observations cannot distinguish competing causes, and generates targeted navigation revisions. Feedback from later goal searches is linked to the rules that produced those revisions and is used to change diagnosis, observation acquisition, and revision planning. The updated improver then governs later navigation improvements, forming a recursive loop in which the system revises its own improvement process. Across goals, the robot conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations are said to validate RPSI-Nav's effectiveness. The abstract does not name the benchmark or report numeric success rates. Numeric tables unread.

title: RoboDx: Repair and Diagnosis of Faults in Robot Software
why: B-type evaluation benchmark in which coding agents repair injected faults in simulated robot navigation software and are judged by a hidden verifier that accepts a repair only if the robot then drives correctly in hidden scenarios the agent never sees, plus a diagnosis track that hides the code.
mechanism: RoboDx generates repair tasks for simulated robot navigation software with known injected faults. A hidden verifier marks a repair as verified only if the robot then drives correctly in hidden scenarios. A second track hides the code and asks the agent to pick the cause from a list of hypotheses. A two-fault task can contain a quiet fault that makes no hidden scenario fail unless the other fault is also present. The authors also give models measurements of each faulty robot, chosen so that only the true cause produces all of them, and compare that setting with giving the simulator's output for every hypothesis.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): on the 100-task set RoboDx-Hard-100, almost every repair by Claude Opus 5.5 with standard coding tools is verified. Of 94 analysed tasks (44 one-fault, 50 two-fault), only 17 of Opus's 49 verified repairs on the 50 two-fault tasks remove both injected edits; most leftover faults are configuration constants whose correct value the task documentation does not state. Opus names both faults on 10/50 of these tasks when it cannot see the code. Four current models given the measurements name the cause on at most 38 of 94 tasks, and are right on almost all when they also get the simulator's output for every hypothesis; their own predictions of that output give no detectable gain. On 97 tasks from real bug-fix pull requests, Claude Haiku 5.5, the weakest model on the generated tasks, scores lowest, and the other three models are not ordered. Numeric tables unread.

title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
why: A-type VLA-agnostic execution-control harness that leaves a frozen short-horizon VLA unchanged, monitors the robot's motion for progress, and adaptively revises the future plan from observed outcomes, evaluated on RoboCasa365, CALVIN, and a Franka Research 3.
mechanism: RePlan-VLA is a framework around an unmodified VLA policy. Rather than asking the VLA to carry long-horizon reasoning, memory, progress tracking, and error recovery, it uses the policy's short-horizon manipulation skills inside an execution-aware loop that monitors motion for progress and revises the future plan from observed outcomes, with no additional fine-tuning of the underlying VLA.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN, success rate improves by 21.9% and 10.4% over the next strongest baseline. The authors also report a real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot. Numeric tables unread; trial counts are not stated in the abstract.

title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
why: B-type (also A-adjacent) benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors, and a custom 3D-printed part; every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course, and agents may revise after watching a video of a real failure.
mechanism: Agents co-design hardware and a control program from a parts kit. Designs that pass in simulation are built and run on a physical obstacle course. Because simulation alone was insufficient (none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course under public part data), an agent can request measurements and watch videos of real runs to learn the simulator. After a video of a real failure, the agent may redesign the robot and sometimes correct its simulator.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots, and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours. Agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms the authors' search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Shown a video of its real failure, an agent removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. Numeric tables unread.

title: Lost Between Mind, Model Collaboration, and Motion: Understanding and Measuring Cross-Model Action Misalignment in Commercial Robots
why: B-type security audit and measurement framework (TARS) for cross-model action misalignment in LLM-controlled commercial robots, where an LLM interprets user intent and a robot-specific action model translates it into physical commands, discovering unintended physical actions even when user inputs contain no explicit action commands.
mechanism: The authors describe a semantic boundary across mind, model collaboration, and motion: consistency may break between what the large model understands, how a smaller action model translates that understanding into executable commands, and what the robot physically does. TARS is a black-box framework that explores this command-reasoning-action pipeline and automatically discovers and validates unintended physical behaviors.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): TARS is evaluated on four commercial robots across 44 experimental settings, with 133,400 executions. The authors report widespread cross-model action misalignment and up to 94% verified action coverage. Robot names, task lists, and numeric tables are not in the abstract.
